The Strategic Cost of Unexamined Explanations Conclusion — Signals Are Necessary, but They Do Not Explain Themselves Product Strategy Evidence Decision Making Strategy Product Signals Don’t Explain Themselves STRIVE Evidence System 7 min read · Oct 11, 2026 -- Listen Share Why accurate customer and product evidence can still lead to incorrect strategic conclusions. STRIVE Evidence Systems | Evidence & Strategy Notes 01 Organizations rarely lack product and customer evidence. They collect transactions, customer interviews, survey responses, support tickets, usage records, conversion rates, retention metrics and experimental results. Yet collecting evidence and interpreting it are different analytical tasks. A company may know precisely how many customers purchased a product, how frequently they returned or how usage changed over time. What remains less certain is which underlying mechanism produced the observed result . This distinction matters because organizations do not make decisions based on numbers alone. They make decisions based on what they believe those numbers mean. A sales increase may justify expansion. Declining usage may trigger product redesign. Strong retention may encourage additional investment. But what happens when the observation is accurate and the explanation attached to it is incomplete or incorrect? The signal can be real while its underlying mechanism remains unresolved. 1. Sales Increase: What Actually Changed? Suppose a company reports a 25% increase in sales. The increase may be accurately measured: revenue may have risen, transactions may have increased, and the dashboard may correctly display the change. But several explanations remain possible: Stronger underlying demand: More customers genuinely need the product, or existing customers now consider it more valuable. Changes in buying frequency: Existing customers are purchasing more often rather than the company necessarily reaching a larger market. Temporary promotional effects: Discounts or incentives accelerated purchases that might otherwise have occurred later. Expanded distribution: New channels or locations made the product accessible to more customers. Changes in competitive conditions: A competitor became temporarily unavailable. Pricing changes: Adjustments affected transaction volume or reported revenue. Each explanation is compatible with some form of sales increase, but they do not establish the same commercial reality . If stronger underlying demand is responsible, the company may reasonably investigate whether additional capacity or market expansion is justified. If temporary promotional activity is responsible, the company should be more cautious about treating the increase as evidence of persistent demand growth. If distribution expansion is responsible, the relevant question may concern channel performance and the sustainability of newly acquired customers. The strategic implications differ because the underlying mechanisms differ. A measured increase establishes that something changed. It does not automatically establish why that change occurred or whether it will persist. 2. Usage Declines: Has Customer Need Weakened? Now consider a digital product experiencing declining feature usage. The organization may interpret the decline as evidence that customers no longer need the feature, leading to redirected resources, postponed development or even feature removal. That interpretation may be correct, but it is not the only possibility. Several mechanisms could explain the same decline: Weaker underlying need: The outcome the feature provides has become less relevant to customers. Greater adoption friction: Additional steps, interface complexity or workflow disruption prevent customers from reaching an outcome they still value. Functional substitution: Another feature now performs the same function more efficiently. Changes in customer composition: A growing customer segment has different needs or usage patterns. Usage can therefore change because of the underlying need, the experience of accessing the solution, the availability of alternatives or the composition of the customer base. These distinctions matter when deciding what to improve. If the underlying need has genuinely weakened, further investment may have limited value. If adoption friction is responsible, improving access or workflow may restore usage without changing the underlying value proposition. If customers have shifted to another feature, the organization may need to reconsider how it measures value across the product rather than attempting to restore usage of the original feature. Declining usage is evidence about observed behavior. It is not, by itself, a complete explanation of customer need. A company that overlooks this distinction risks withdrawing support from something customers still value — or continuing to optimize a feature whose relevance has genuinely diminished. 3. Strong Retention: What Keeps Customers Returning? Retention is often treated as a reassuring indicator of product performance. Customers continue purchasing, renewing subscriptions or maintaining their relationships with a company, and the organization may interpret this as evidence of strong product value and customer satisfaction. Sometimes that interpretation is well supported. Customers may continue because the product reliably solves an important problem, delivers meaningful outcomes and remains preferable to available alternatives.
